'''Robert "Bob" Lynn Carroll''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|CM|FRSC}}  (May 5, 1938 – April 7, 2020) was an American–Canadian [[vertebrate paleontologist]] who specialised in [[Paleozoic]] and [[Mesozoic]] [[amphibian]]s and [[reptile]]s.<ref name="Sues-Murray-Anderson">{{cite journal |last=Sues |first=Hans-Dieter |author-link=Hans-Dieter Sues |author2=Murray, A.M. |author3=Anderson, J.S. |year=2003 |title=Robert Lynn Carroll — an appreciation |journal=Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=469–472 |url=http://pubs.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/rp/rppdf/e02-098.pdf |doi=10.1139/e02-098 |bibcode=2003CaJES..40..469S |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050515104708/http://pubs.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/rp/rppdf/e02-098.pdf |archive-date=2005-05-15 }}</ref>

== Biography ==
Carroll was an only child and grew up on a [[farm]] near [[Lansing, Michigan]]. He was introduced to [[paleontology]] by his [[father]] shortly after his fifth [[birthday]], and by the time he was eight he had decided he wanted to be a [[vertebrate paleontologist]]. In that same year he received as a Christmas present the left [[femur]] of an ''[[Allosaurus]]'', courtesy of [[Edwin H. Colbert]], whom his father had told about his interest.<ref name="science.ca">{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.ca/scientists/scientistprofile.php?pID=335|title=science.ca: Robert L. Carroll|website=www.science.ca}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.vertpaleo.org/meetings/2004romersimpsonmedalwinner.cfm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100716014457/http://www.vertpaleo.org/meetings/2004romersimpsonmedalwinner.cfm |title=2004 A. S. Romer-G. G. Simpson Medal|archive-date=July 16, 2010}}</ref> In his teen years his parents took him on many fossil hunting trips to [[Wyoming]] and [[South Dakota]].

After high-school, he went to [[Michigan State University]], where he received a B.Sc. in 1959, majoring in [[Geology]].<ref name=":0" /> From there he went to [[Harvard University]] where he studied [[biology]] and [[palaeontology]] under [[Alfred Sherwood Romer]] for his M.A. (1961) and Ph.D. degrees (1963); Carroll was Romer's last student.<ref name="Sues-Murray-Anderson"/><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Caldwell|first1=Michael|last2=Larsson|first2=Hans|date=2020-05-04|title=Robert "Bob" Lynn Carroll (1938 - 2020): The 'academic ancestor' of Canadian vertebrate palaeontology|url=https://journals.library.ualberta.ca/vamp/index.php/VAMP/article/view/29364|journal=Vertebrate Anatomy Morphology Palaeontology|volume=8|pages=1–6|doi=10.18435/vamp29364|issn=2292-1389|doi-access=free}}</ref> His doctoral thesis dealt with what is now known as [[Dissorophoidea]], a group of Paleozoic [[amphibian]]s that are often considered the closest relatives of [[Lissamphibia|present day amphibians]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Anderson|first=Jason S.|date=2008-11-12|title=Focal Review: The Origin(s) of Modern Amphibians|journal=Evolutionary Biology|volume=35|issue=4|pages=231–247|doi=10.1007/s11692-008-9044-5|bibcode=2008EvBio..35..231A |s2cid=44050103|issn=0071-3260}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=SIGURDSEN|first1=TROND|last2=GREEN|first2=DAVID M.|date=2011-01-21|title=The origin of modern amphibians: a re-evaluation|journal=Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=162|issue=2|pages=457–469|doi=10.1111/j.1096-3642.2010.00683.x|issn=0024-4082|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pardo|first1=Jason D.|last2=Small|first2=Bryan J.|last3=Huttenlocker|first3=Adam K.|date=2017-06-19|title=Stem caecilian from the Triassic of Colorado sheds light on the origins of Lissamphibia|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=114|issue=27|pages=E5389–E5395|doi=10.1073/pnas.1706752114|pmid=28630337|pmc=5502650|bibcode=2017PNAS..114E5389P |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref> although they may also be [[Stem tetrapoda|stem-tetrapods]] if lissamphibians instead arose from within [[Lepospondyli]].<ref>{{Citation|last1=Laurin|first1=Michel|date=1997|title=Amniote Origins|pages=9–59|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-12-676460-4|last2=Reisz|first2=Robert R.|chapter=A New Perspective on Tetrapod Phylogeny|doi=10.1016/b978-012676460-4/50003-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Marjanović|first1=David|last2=Laurin|first2=Michel|date=2007-06-01|title=Fossils, Molecules, Divergence Times, and the Origin of Lissamphibians|journal=Systematic Biology|volume=56|issue=3|pages=369–388|doi=10.1080/10635150701397635|pmid=17520502|issn=1076-836X|doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Pyron|first=R. Alexander|date=2011-05-03|title=Divergence Time Estimation Using Fossils as Terminal Taxa and the Origins of Lissamphibia|journal=Systematic Biology|volume=60|issue=4|pages=466–481|doi=10.1093/sysbio/syr047|pmid=21540408|issn=1076-836X|doi-access=free}}</ref>

After obtaining his [[Ph.D.]], Carroll held a [[National Research Council (Canada)|National Research Council]] (NRC) [[postdoctoral fellowship]] at [[Redpath Museum]] at [[McGill University]] in [[Montreal]] (1962-1963), and then a [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) postdoctoral position at the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] in [[London]].<ref name="Sues-Murray-Anderson" />  During this [[time]], he studied [[tetrapod]] remains from the [[Pennsylvanian (geology)|Pennsylvanian]] lycopod "tree stumps" at [[Joggins, Nova Scotia]] (a variety of [[Temnospondyli|temnospondyls]], [[Microsauria|microsaurs]], and [[Basal (phylogenetics)|basal]] [[amniote]]s). Most of this material was collected and first studied by [[John William Dawson|Sir William Dawson]], the first Principal of McGill University, in the nineteenth century.<ref name="Sues-Murray-Anderson"/>

Returning from [[London]], in 1964 Carroll joined the permanent staff of [[McGill University]] as curator of geology at the [[Redpath Museum]] and became the curator of [[vertebrate paleontology]] the following year.<ref name="science.ca"/><ref name=":2" /> At McGill, he was an assistant professor of zoology from 1964 to 1969, an associate professor of biology from 1969-1974, a full professor from 1974 onwards, and was appointed Strathcona Professor of Zoology in 1987.<ref name="Sues-Murray-Anderson"/><ref name=":2" />  From 1985 to 1991 he was director of the [[Redpath Museum]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mcgill.ca/redpath/about/directors|title=Directors of the Museum, Past and Present|website=Redpath Museum}}</ref> He was an active professor until 2003, after which he was an emeritus professor.

Carroll died on April 7, 2020, at the St. Margaret Residential Centre in [[Westmount, Quebec]], of complications from [[COVID-19]]. He suffered from [[Alzheimer]] in his last years.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/covid-19-has-taken-our-parents-our-grandparents-our-friends-here-are-a-few-to-help-remember-the-many|title=COVID-19 has taken our parents, our grandparents, our friends. Here are a few, to help remember the many &#124; National Post|date=April 25, 2020}}</ref> He was survived by his wife, Anna Di Turi, a [[retired]] [[business school]] [[teacher]], and his one child, David, and granddaughter Juliette.

== Scientific research ==
Carroll was a prolific publisher and studied numerous major topics within paleontology and vertebrate evolution. He is best known for his work addressing the origins and early evolution of amphibians<ref>{{Cite journal|last=CARROLL|first=ROBERT L.|date=2007|title=The Palaeozoic Ancestry of Salamanders, Frogs and Caecilians|journal=Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=150|issue=suppl_1|pages=1–140|doi=10.1111/j.1096-3642.2007.00246.x|issn=1096-3642|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite Development|volume=5|issue=3|pages=314–324|doi=10.1046/j.1525-142x.2003.03038.x|pmid=12752770|s2cid=22067298|issn=1520-541X}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=Carroll|first=Robert L.|title=Patterns of Evolution as Illustrated by the Fossil Record|chapter=Chapter 13 Patterns of Amphibian Evolution: An Extended Example of the Incompleteness of the Fossil Several taxa are named after Carroll, including the teleost fish ''Mahengecharax carrolli,'' the '[[Microsauria|microsaurs]]' ''[[Bolterpeton|Bolterpeton carrolli]]'' (now a synonym of the [[Parareptilia|parareptile]] ''Delorhynchus'') and ''[[Carrolla|Carrolla craddocki]]'', and the [[Captorhinidae|captorhinid]] ''[[Opisthodontosaurus|Opisthodontosaurus carrolli]].'' He was honored with a [[festschrift]] in 2003.<ref name="Sues-Murray-Anderson" />

Carroll was awarded a large number of awards, including the [[Charles Schuchert Award]] of the [[Paleontological Society]] (1978), of which he was one of the first recipients, the Elkanah Billings Medal of the [[Geological Association of Canada]] (1991), the [[Willet G. Miller Medal]] of the [[Royal Society of Canada]] (2001), of which he was made an honorary member in 1993, and the Romer-Simpson Medal of the [[Society of Vertebrate Paleontology]] (2004), the society's most prestigious honor,<ref name=":1" /> and was appointed a member of the [[Order of Canada]] (2019).<ref>{{Cite news|last=Dunlevy|first=T'Cha|date=2019-06-27|title=Alanis Obomsawin, 15 other Quebecers to receive Order of Canada|language=en|newspaper=Montreal Gazette|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/16-quebecers-to-receive-order-of-canada-honours|url-status=live|access-date=2019-07-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190704041620/https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/16-quebecers-to-receive-order-of-canada-honours|archive-date=2019-07-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=General|first=Office of the Secretary to the Governor|date=2019-06-20|title=Governor General Announces 83 New Appointments to the Order of Canada|url=https://www.gg.ca/en/media/news/2019/governor-general-announces-83-new-appointments-order-canada|access-date=2020-12-25|website=The Governor General of Canada|archive-date=2019-06-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190628034534/https://www.gg.ca/en/media/news/2019/governor-general-announces-83-new-appointments-order-canada}}</ref> Carroll also served as the president of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology from 1982 to 1983.<ref>{{Cite web|title=SVP - Past Presidents|url=http://vertpaleo.org/the-Society/Leadership/SVP_Past_Presidents.aspx|access-date=2020-12-25|archive-date=2019-06-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190607194232/http://vertpaleo.org/The-Society/Leadership/SVP_Past_Presidents.aspx}}</ref> The Canadian Society of Vertebrate Paleontology's Carroll Prize is named after Carroll.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-02-24|title=Robert Lynn Carroll Prize|url=https://csvp.ca/awards-2/carroll-prize/|access-date=2020-12-25|language=en}}</ref>

Carroll is often credited with being the "father of Canadian vertebrate paleontology"<ref name=":1" /> because many contemporary Canadian paleontologists can trace their graduate training back to him. Carroll supervised numerous graduate students, many of whom went on to lead their own successful research labs, including Jason Anderson ([[University of Calgary]]), Michael Caldwell ([[University of Alberta]]), [[Philip J. Currie|Philip Currie]] (University of Alberta), and [[Robert R. Reisz|Robert Reisz]] ([[University of Toronto]]).
